client: I've been really struggling ever since my dad passed away two months ago — it was so sudden, and I just wasn't prepared for any of it. Everything that used to feel normal or even enjoyable just feels kind of hollow now, like I'm going through the motions. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep living like this.
therapist:
I'm really glad you reached out, and it takes genuine courage to try something new when you're already feeling so depleted. What you're describing — that hollowness, going through the motions — makes complete sense after such a sudden, profound loss, and it doesn't mean something is permanently broken in you. I also want to honor your honesty about doubting whether talking will help, because that skepticism is worth holding alongside the part of you that showed up here anyway.

Can you tell me a little about what a typical day has felt like for you these past two months?

client: Honestly, most days I just kind of drag myself through the basics — get up, go to work, come home, stare at my phone or the TV without really taking anything in. I used to call my dad pretty much every Sunday, and now Sunday rolls around and I just don't know what to do with myself, so I usually end up just lying in bed longer than I should. It's like there's this routine-shaped hole where he used to be, and I keep almost reaching for it out of habit and then remembering all over again.
therapist:
That image of a "routine-shaped hole" is such a vivid and honest way to describe what you're experiencing — grief doesn't just live in big moments, it hides in the small, ordinary ones like a Sunday phone call, and that repeated moment of reaching and remembering must be exhausting in a quiet, relentless way. What you're feeling isn't you failing to cope; it's actually a reflection of how real and meaningful that connection with your dad was. 

I'm curious — when Sunday comes and that wave hits, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, a lot of it is guilt — like, I keep thinking about the last time we talked and whether I said enough, whether he knew how much I appreciated him. I also get this thought that I should have called more often, not just on Sundays, and now it's too late and there's nothing I can do about that. It's like my brain just keeps circling back to all the things I didn't do rather than letting me just... miss him.
therapist:
That circling your brain does — replaying what you didn't say or do — is such a common but painful part of grief, and it's worth gently noticing that your mind is essentially trying to find a way to fix something that feels unbearable, even when there's nothing left to fix. The fact that you're so focused on whether he *knew* you appreciated him actually tells me a lot about how much you cared — people who don't love deeply don't tend to worry about this the way you do. 

I'd like to explore that thought a little — if you imagine your dad looking at the relationship you two had, the Sunday calls, the consistency of showing up week after week, what do you think *he* would say about whether you loved him enough?

client: I mean, logically I know he probably would have said I was a good kid and that he knew I loved him — he wasn't the type to hold things against people. But when I try to actually picture that, it feels almost like I'm just making it up to make myself feel better, like I'm putting words in his mouth that I can't really be sure of. So I'm not sure that exercise fully works for me, because my brain just comes back with "but you can't actually know that."
therapist:
That's such an important and honest pushback, and I really respect that you're not just accepting a reframe that doesn't genuinely land for you — that kind of self-awareness is actually really valuable in this process. What I'd gently offer is that your brain applying that "you can't actually know" standard only seems to go one direction — it doubts the reassuring thoughts, but it accepts the guilty ones as fact, even though you can't fully verify those either. 

So I'm wondering — what actual evidence from your *history together*, things he said or did over the years, might speak to how he saw you and your relationship?

client: That point about the double standard actually kind of stopped me for a second, because I hadn't thought about it that way before. I guess there are things — like he used to brag about me to his friends, I know that because they'd mention it, and he'd always pick up the phone no matter what time I called. But even as I'm saying that, there's a part of me that feels almost guilty for using those memories as evidence, like I'm trying to let myself off the hook for something I should still feel bad about.
therapist:
That moment of pause you just had is really significant — you found real, concrete evidence that existed independent of your grief, things other people witnessed and reflected back to you. And I want to name what's happening in that last part gently: your mind seems to have a rule that feeling better about this is somehow a betrayal, like grief is something you *owe* your dad, and that letting go of the guilt means you're not taking the loss seriously enough.

What do you think — is it possible to fully honor how much he meant to you *and* release some of this guilt, or does part of you feel those two things can't coexist?

client: That framing actually makes a strange kind of sense — like I've been treating the guilt as proof that I loved him, so dropping it feels dangerous, like I'd be losing the last thread connecting me to how much he mattered. But I genuinely don't know how you just... decide to let something like that go, it's not like I can flip a switch. It feels more like the guilt has become such a habit that even if I wanted to release it, I wouldn't know where to start.
therapist:
What you just named — guilt as a habit, as a thread of connection — is genuinely one of the most insightful things you can recognize in grief, and it reframes the whole challenge: this isn't about willpower or flipping a switch, it's about slowly building *other* threads that connect you to how much he mattered, ones that don't require you to suffer to prove your love. The Sunday calls, the bragging to his friends, the way he always picked up — those are also threads, and they don't ask anything painful of you to hold onto. 

I'm wondering if we could think small here — is there one tiny thing, maybe even on a Sunday, that might let you feel close to him or honor what he meant to you in a way that feels different from lying in bed with the guilt?

client: There's a part of me that wants to say yes to that, but I'm also a little worried that whatever I try will just end up feeling hollow or performative, like I'm doing a ritual that doesn't actually reach him. He and I used to watch the same football team, and I've been avoiding games completely because it feels like too much — but maybe that's actually something I could try, just watching a game and letting myself think about him without it having to mean anything profound. I guess my hesitation is that I'm not sure if it'll help or just make the missing worse.
therapist:
What you just described — watching a game, letting yourself think about him, without it needing to be profound — actually sounds like exactly the right size and spirit for a first step, and I love that it came from you rather than me. And your hesitation is worth taking seriously, but I'd gently offer that "making the missing worse" and "helping" might not be opposites here — sometimes letting yourself truly miss someone in a context that also holds good memories is itself a form of relief, even when it hurts.

What if you approached it as a small experiment rather than a solution — just one game, with no pressure to feel better afterward, and then we see what actually happened rather than what you feared might happen?

client: Framing it as an experiment rather than a solution actually takes some pressure off, because I think part of what's been stopping me is this fear that I'll try something and it won't work and that'll just confirm that nothing can help. I can probably do that — just one game, no expectations. I guess my only real worry is that I'll be sitting there alone, and the loneliness of watching it without being able to text him about it might just feel unbearable in a way that's hard to prepare for.
therapist:
That worry about the loneliness mid-game is so real and worth taking seriously — there's a difference between missing him in the abstract and hitting that specific moment where you'd normally grab your phone, and it makes sense to think ahead about that. It might be worth having a small plan for that moment, not to avoid the feeling but to have somewhere to put it — whether that's texting a friend who knew him, jotting down what you would have said to him, or just letting yourself sit with it for a minute and acknowledging that the urge to reach out is itself evidence of something beautiful.

Is there anyone in your life — maybe someone who also loved him or shared that football connection — who might want to watch that game with you, or even just be a text away?

client: There's my uncle — my dad's brother — who's been a fan of the same team forever, and honestly I've been avoiding him a little because talking to him means talking about my dad, and I haven't felt ready for that. But maybe that's actually backwards, like maybe he's one of the few people who actually gets what I'm losing because he's losing it too. I'm a little scared to reach out because I don't want to make it harder for him or feel like I'm burdening someone else with my grief.
therapist:
What you just flipped there — realizing that avoiding your uncle might actually be backwards — is a really meaningful shift, and I think your instinct is right that he might be one of the few people who doesn't need the loss explained to him. And that fear of burdening him is tender and kind, but consider that he may be sitting with his own version of the same loneliness, possibly also wondering if reaching out would be too much for *you* — sometimes two people are protecting each other from the very thing they both need.

What would it feel like to send him just a small, low-pressure message — maybe something as simple as mentioning the game and seeing if he'd want to watch together?

client: Honestly, when I picture actually typing that message out, my stomach tightens up a little — like there's this fear that once I open that door, we'll both just fall apart and I won't know how to hold that for either of us. But I think you're right that we might both be doing the same dance around each other, and that's kind of a sad thought. I could probably manage something short, like just mentioning the game without making it heavy, and see what he says.
therapist:
That image of both of you doing the same dance around each other, each trying to protect the other, is quietly heartbreaking — and noticing it might be exactly what gives you the courage to take one small step out of it. A short, light message about the game is a beautiful way to open a door without forcing either of you to walk through it all at once, and if you both end up falling apart a little watching that game together, that might actually be exactly the right thing rather than something to fear.

As you sit with all of this today, I'm wondering — what feels even just slightly different about how you're seeing things compared to when we started talking?
